A1.justification: Both PDFs describe LLM-Streamline. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding methods, equations, experiments, and results can be matched despite substantial reformatting and relocation.

before.justification: v3 reports original pruning experiments on Llama2-7B and OPT models, including benchmark evaluations, replacement-network ablations, pruning-ratio analyses, and a LoRA comparison.

after.justification: v4 retains original experiments and adds Llama2-13B and Baichuan evaluations, calibration-data sensitivity tests, and a larger-data post-training study.

M1.justification: Both versions select contiguous layers using hidden-state cosine similarity and train a lightweight replacement using MSE. The replacement architectures, initialization alternatives, and optional language-model post-training remain unchanged; additional comparisons and explanations do not introduce a new method component.

E1.justification: The classification and generation benchmarks, including the smaller-OPT benchmark suite, are retained. v4 Appendix A adds Wikitext and standalone C4 calibration scenarios alongside SlimPajama to test pruning-data sensitivity. The additional model families do not introduce new downstream tasks or languages.

E2.justification: v4 Appendix A adds an evaluated perplexity-based pruning comparator explicitly identified as SLEB in Table 9. Existing LLM-Pruner, SliceGPT, LaCo, and LoRA comparisons remain. Shortened Llama appears in the related-work comparison table but receives no new performance evaluation.

E3.justification: v4 adds Llama2-13B and four Baichuan/Baichuan2 model configurations, plus a 5.49M-sample post-training condition. The reported LoRA protocol changes from rank 384 to 128, 30,000 to 300,000 training samples, ten epochs to one, and learning rate 5e-5 to 1e-4 (Section 4.7 and training appendices). These are substantive setting changes, not evidence of a same-setting performance comparison.

E4.justification: New Appendix A tests whether cosine- and perplexity-based pruning select consistent layers across calibration corpora and preserve downstream performance. New Appendix D.5 tests whether substantially more post-training data improves recovery and at what computational cost. Earlier architecture, initialization, and pruning-ratio analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests for benchmark results. The existing perplexity standard deviations used to construct the stability metric remain unchanged and are not estimates of uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial results for Llama2-13B, Baichuan models, calibration sensitivity, and training-data scaling. For example, Llama2-13B FFN reports 53.2 average classification accuracy and 84.9 stability. Under revised settings, Table 6 replaces LoRA accuracy/stability of 44.6/82.6 with 44.5/82.1 and GPU memory of 47.6 G with 56.4 G. Earlier main Llama2-7B and OPT results are retained.

T1.justification: Equations 1–6 retain the same residual-layer formulation, cosine criterion, MSE objective, confidence statistic, and stability definition. No theorem, proof, or substantive mathematical derivation is added; the new methodological discussions are conceptual explanations.

C1.justification: The pruning-and-replacement and stability contributions remain central. v4 extends the headline retention claim from 7B to 7B or 13B models and explicitly claims training-efficiency advantages over concurrent pruning methods, broadening the earlier emphasis on accuracy and stability.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations based on hidden-state magnitude and calibration-data sensitivity for choosing cosine similarity, and recasts replacement versus LoRA as local knowledge recovery versus redistribution across remaining layers. It qualifies the earlier GSM8K failure observation with recovery under more training, discusses the associated cost, and adds Appendix E's stated limitation relative to quantization.

D1.justification: v4 revises the documented LoRA hyperparameters, lists selected layer indices in Table 8, and specifies the full-data training size and reported computational cost. Captions clarify that dagger-marked networks halve the intermediate dimension. Existing replacement-training hyperparameters, A800 hardware information, and data-mixture proportions are retained.

R1.justification: The brief earlier positioning is expanded into a detailed comparison with concurrent layer-pruning approaches, including newly cited SLEB and Shortened Llama. Table 7 contrasts selection criteria, training requirements, data, and trained modules. Existing ShortGPT and UIDL references receive substantially fuller treatment, and additional literature supports the cosine-similarity rationale.

P1.justification: The introduction, methodological discussion, results narrative, and related-work section are extensively rewritten. Sections 4.5–4.7 gain explicit takeaway statements, appendices are reorganized, and citation style and terminology are revised. These changes extend beyond inserting new experimental material.

P2.justification: Main Tables 2–4 now pair Llama2-7B with Llama2-13B, while the original OPT-6.7B blocks move into separate appendix tables. New tables display concurrent-method characteristics, calibration comparisons, Baichuan results, and data scaling. Figures receive styling and legend updates, alongside a different document header and heading layout.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens validation through larger and additional model families and direct tests of previously untested pruning-criterion and training-data choices. Appendix D.5 also qualifies v3's mathematical-task failure observation by documenting partial recovery and its reported 100-fold computational cost. Expanded research positioning and an explicit quantization limitation clarify scope. Broader efficiency claims still lack uniform matched comparisons, and the revised LoRA scores are not directly comparable across versions, but the additions resolve important empirical validation gaps.
